title: Vesali is lovely
hook: he looks back at the city turning his whole body, like an elephant, and says how delightful it was (DN 16)

segments.voice: Yesterday, be an island: no successor, just the dhamma, and your own ground. Your line was be your own island. What did you decide yourself? Day eighty.

The last time you left a place you loved, did you look back? The apartment, emptied out, keys on the counter. A hometown in the rearview mirror. A hospital room. Most of us do. We turn around at the door. Vesali was a rich, lively city, full of shrines and gardens and a proud, independent people. The Buddha had spent many seasons there. It was where the women had walked to ask for ordination. Where a famous courtesan named Ambapali had given him a mango grove and a meal, beating the city's princes to the invitation. And in the last months of his life, the old texts show him in Vesali, enjoying it.
screen: `DID YOU LOOK BACK?` → `VESALI, A LIVELY CITY.` → `IN HIS LAST MONTHS, ENJOYING IT.`

segments.voice: It's one of the loveliest surprises in the whole account. One day, sitting at a shrine outside the city, the Buddha turns to Ananda and simply names the places he loves. Delightful is Vesali, Ananda. Delightful is this shrine, and that one, and that one, and he lists them by name. An awakened man, near the end of his life, enjoying the view. Some people imagine that letting go means not caring about anything. Being above it all. This moment says something else. He's free of clinging, and he can still say, this place is beautiful. Maybe that's exactly why he can say it so simply, without needing to keep it. Then comes the leaving. After his last alms round in Vesali, as he walks away, he stops and turns to look back at the city. And the text says he turned his whole body around, the way an elephant does. An elephant can't just glance over its shoulder; it turns its whole great body to look. The Pali has a word for it: the elephant look. And he says to Ananda: this is the last time I will look at Vesali. That's all. No speech about impermanence, though he'd taught it a thousand times. He just turns, fully, and looks. Then he turns back, and walks on. Two things held together, again. He loves it. He lets it go. Both, completely. Nothing half-turned. You could spend a lifetime learning to look at anything that way.
screen: `DELIGHTFUL IS VESALI.` · `FREE OF CLINGING, STILL LOVING.` · `THE ELEPHANT LOOK.` · `THE LAST TIME I'LL SEE IT.` · then, large: `HOW LOVELY IT WAS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look back fondly at one place. Settle and breathe. Bring to mind a place you loved and left. A childhood kitchen. A school. A city. A friend's porch. Walk through it slowly in your mind. See the light. Hear it. Then, the way an elephant turns, turn your whole attention toward it, and say quietly: how lovely it was. Let it be lovely. Then let it be past. The bell holds the time.
Vesali is lovely. The Buddha naming the places he loved, and turning his whole body, like an elephant, for one last look.
Your line: how lovely it was. Today, when you leave somewhere, turn fully around at the door and look once, before you go. Day eighty.

howItsDone: Pilgrims still visit Vaishali in Bihar, India, where an Ashokan pillar and stupa ruins mark places tied to the Buddha's life, and the 'elephant look' is remembered in the Mahaparinibbana Sutta, read across Buddhist traditions.

fork.setup: you're leaving a city you love for the last time, and you know it. what do you do?
options: turn your whole body and look, then walk on.
fork.reveal: he turns fully, like an elephant, and says: this is the last time I'll look at Vesali. then he walks on.

original.note: Pali: the elephant look. Naga (elephant) and apalokita (looking back).

trapdoor: what you thought: an old man feeling nostalgic.
what it means: love and letting go held completely at once, in one full turn of the body.
what a scholar hears: DN 16, 3.2 (ramaniya Vesali) and 4.1 (nagapalokitam apaloketva); later Buddhist art and texts treat the elephant look as a mark of a Buddha.
